What We Did: Replace placeholders with NaN and handle missing required fields
Why: Placeholders like 'unknown' or '-' are not real measurements. If the regression treats them as data, it learns patterns from fabricated values and its predictions of Economic Loss become unreliable.

Duplicate rows give the same observation extra weight during training, so the regression overfits to those records and the learned coefficients no longer reflect the true relationship between the predictors and Economic Loss.

If 'France' and 'france ' stay as different labels, one-hot encoding splits the same country into two columns, each with half the rows. The regression then estimates two weaker country effects instead of one reliable effect on Economic Loss.
A regression can only compute with numeric inputs. Text in a numeric column would either be dropped or cause an error, so the affected rows could not contribute to predicting Economic Loss.
Negative waste or a household share above 100% cannot occur in reality. Left in, they pull the regression line toward impossible relationships and distort the predicted loss for otherwise valid rows.

A row without Economic Loss has no target value, so supervised regression cannot learn from it. A row without Country or Food Category cannot be encoded, so it would either crash the model or be silently dropped later.

What We Did: Review unusual values without automatic removal
Why: Some flagged values may be genuine (large countries genuinely waste more). Removing them automatically would bias the regression toward mid-sized cases and make the model under-predict loss for the largest countries.

The same country and year appears with many different population values (e.g., France ranges from 93 to 1,376 million within the same year), some values are negative, and a single threshold cannot separate realistic values for large countries from impossible values for small ones. Left in, the regression would learn from fabricated values and could output misleading country-level loss estimates.
